learning_outcomes.text: Correctly and fluently handle logarithmic units of power, gain, and attenuation used in communication systems.
Apply the fundamentals of time and frequency domain analysis to solve problems in communication systems.
Characterize information, as a signal and as a stochastic process, to be transmitted by a communication system, as well as the disturbances that limit the performance of said system.
Describe and distinguish the functional blocks of analog and digital communication systems.
Obtain the fundamental parameters of analog and digital communication systems.
Understand the limitations and performance of different analog and digital modulation systems.
Conveniently evaluate the trade-off between bandwidth and power consumption to achieve a certain quality in a given analog or digital communication system configuration.
Assimilate the fundamentals of decision theory and signal space to apply them in solving signal detection problems in digital communication systems.
Understand the main analog and digital modulation techniques to identify the most appropriate technique in a given transmission configuration.
Discuss and evaluate in a group the most appropriate analog and/or digital modulation technique under given operating conditions and restrictions.
Apply knowledge of different technological alternatives for deploying communication systems to functionally design systems that meet certain pre-imposed requirements and performance.

syllabus_topics: Tools and useful parameters in digital communication systems. Digital communication system model. Signal and noise representation in signal space. Gram-Schmidt algorithm. Decision criteria. Symbol and bit error probability. Q function and its properties. Error probability bounds. Parameters related to error probability: Eb/N0, Ec/N0, C/N, S/N. Approximate calculation of Eb/N0 for generic constellations. Power gain of one modulation over another. Spectral and power efficiency. Hartley-Shannon formula and Shannon channel capacity limit.

Systems based on amplitude and/or phase modulations under Gaussian channels. Generic block diagram. Conditions for no inter-symbol interference (ISI). Nyquist criterion and consequences. Minimum bandwidth. Raised cosine pulses. Consequences of truncation. Eye diagram. Analysis of amplitude and/or phase modulations (PAM, QAM, PSK, QPSK, OQPSK and DPSK): temporal, spectral and signal space representation, error probability in Gaussian channel, spectral and power efficiency. Example: DVB-S.
Detection of amplitude and/or phase modulated signals in linear channels. Equivalent discrete channel. ML sequence detector. Viterbi algorithm.

Systems based on multi-carrier modulations. Introduction and motivation. Conditions for no ISI in Gaussian channels. Continuous and discrete time systems for Gaussian channels. Parameters of interest and results for Gaussian channels. Equivalent 1-D and L-D discrete channel. Continuous and discrete time systems for linear channels. Spectral representation. Example: DVB-T.
Systems based on frequency modulations. Systems based on FSK and CPFSK. Phase tree. OQPSK representation of MSK modulation. Error probability in Gaussian channels. Spectral and power efficiency.

Systems based on spread spectrum modulations. Direct sequence spread spectrum (DSSS). Generation and detection. Equivalent discrete channel. Frequency hopping spread spectrum (FH). Design of chirp sequences.
assessment_rules: In the ordinary call, the final grade is the sum of the Theory Block (BT) and the Practical Block (BP). The BT accounts for 60% of the final grade and is obtained from a single written theory exam (ET) scored out of 6 points, with no minimum required. The BP accounts for 40% of the final grade and is obtained from two laboratory projects, each weighing 20% of the final grade. Each project includes online questionnaires (C), class participation (PC), and a practical exam (EP), weighted 6%, 24%, and 70% respectively for the project grade, with no minimums required for these components. In the extraordinary call, students can choose between two options for the practical block: either take a new individual theoretical-practical practical exam (EP), which will count for 40% of the final grade, or keep the BP score obtained in the ordinary call. For students under differentiated evaluation, the theory exam (ET) accounts for 100% of the final grade, with the score scaled by 10/6. In case of doubt regarding authorship or unauthorized means, a presential defense may be requested.
